patient_information: The patient is a 55-year-old indigenous Australian woman. She has been living in a crowded back room of a house in a remote community.
chief_complaint: Widespread exfoliating rash and signs of sepsis.
history_of_present_illness: The patient's family reported that she had become increasingly withdrawn and had not been getting out of the house much at all prior to presentation.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient resides in a remote indigenous community in tropical northern Australia where scabies is endemic. She was living in a crowded back room. Many household members, particularly children, were found to have multiple scabies lesions, some with secondary pyoderma, indicating she was a 'core transmitter'.
vitals: Temperature was 39.5°C (103.1°F), heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, and blood pressure was 85 mmHg systolic. Oxygen saturation was 92% on room air.
physical_exam: The patient was pale, clammy, and poorly responsive. She had a widespread exfoliative rash involving all limbs, with particular severity in the armpits, buttocks, and thighs. Numerous skin flakes were present on her mattress. She also had fissures over her wrists and knees.
labs_and_diagnostics: Microscopy of skin scrapings confirmed the diagnosis, showing multiple scabies mites of varying maturity and multiple eggs. Initial blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus resistant to flucloxacillin and clindamycin but sensitive to gentamicin, co-trimoxazole, and doxycycline (community-acquired MRSA). Repeated blood cultures 48 hours after admission were negative. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no features of endocarditis.
differential_diagnosis: The primary provisional diagnosis was crusted scabies, given the classical exfoliating rash in a patient from an endemic community. Secondary sepsis was also diagnosed, with the likely cause being Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes bacteremia from inoculation through skin fissures. Gram-negative or polymicrobial sepsis were also considered possibilities.
management_and_clinical_course: Initial management included oxygen, a wide-bore cannula, 1 litre of normal saline, and intravenous ceftriaxone and gentamicin. After stabilization, she was evacuated to a regional hospital and managed in a single room with contact precautions. Treatment for scabies consisted of a five-dose course of ivermectin (200 μg/kg/dose) combined with topical benzyl benzoate and a keratolytic cream. Following culture results, she was treated with two weeks of IV vancomycin for the MRSA bacteremia. She became afebrile and was off oxygen within 48 hours. After three weeks, her skin showed no residual hyperkeratosis and she returned to her community. Her family members were also treated for scabies.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was crusted scabies with secondary sepsis caused by community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). The crusted scabies was confirmed by microscopy of skin scrapings showing numerous mites and eggs. The secondary MRSA bacteremia was confirmed by blood cultures. The patient showed significant clinical improvement and resolution of skin lesions following targeted treatment with ivermectin, topical scabicides, and intravenous vancomycin.
